Neurologica: The Stats on Police Killings[7]
sections.title: Question #1: Policing and Race

sections.text: We had numerous, numerous questions on this study, which is why I think we need to break it down a little bit. So this has to do with statistics on police use of force and police killings. I think, unfortunately, one slice of this study is being often discussed without putting it in the full context of the whole study, which is what I wanted to do. This was actually a Harvard professor—an economics professor, who used an economics model, and also did a lot of data collection for this study—focusing on different cities around the United States. So it’s not using federal-level data, and it’s important to note that the one thing that researchers all agree on is we don’t have enough data; we need better tracking systems for all police use of force as well as police shootings and people who die at the hands of police so that we can do good statistical analysis. But this was a big study. And the professor and people who did this study were actually a little bit surprised by the results, which I always find is a good thing. It means that they were looking at the data and not—you know, when it goes against their preconceived notions, it’s harder to think that they were working backwards from their conclusion.

So, in any case, the thing that’s been widely reported—and what we got most of the questions on—was that the study—if you look just at people who are killed by police officers during the time of the study in the United States, and then you look at all the different factors that might influence—that correlate with that, they were unable to show that the race of the victim, the person who was killed, is an independent variable. In other words, in this data set, cops were not killing black people at a higher rate than white people once you control for a lot of other things, such as the number of times people are interacting with the police, the crime rate, all those things. So that’s what people are saying. Like, "Therefore, is it not true, then, that there isn’t evidence of systemic racism in policing?" (Transcriptionist's note: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence!) That conclusion goes way beyond that one slice of data, and it’s interesting that if you just read through this study, there’s lots of other things that it reports on that show very clearly that there is [systemic] racism in policing.[note 1] The same data, for example, showed a very robust signal that the use of non-lethal force is consistently higher against Black Americans than not-Black Americans—White Americans, for example.
And also, Steve, that’s just reported uses. You have to remember that, too. Yeah, that’s only what we know.

Yeah, so that’s, of course, one of the caveats in the data. The data is not—although these researchers did go to great lengths to scour those reports—but, yes, there’s no system of systematically reporting such things, and so—
—Yeah, the thing is, if it was never reported, they were never going to have that.

Yeah, right. It’s missing from the data. But even in the data that we have, it’s across the board: for every kind of use of non-lethal force—such as handcuffing, tasing, physically touching, pushing to the ground, all those things—there were higher [instances], across the cities in the study, for Black Americans than White Americans. And that was an independent variable that could not be explained by all the other variables that they looked at. It looked like a completely independent variable. But here’s the other thing: there was much more data, there were many, many more instances of use of non-lethal force than the use of lethal force. Also, you could break the use of lethal force down into two categories: looking at instances where the person killed was armed—so the police were shooting an armed suspect—and you could break out just situations where the person was unarmed. Now, that’s a smaller group, right?
Oh is it? Interesting. That’s smaller.
Oh, it’s much smaller! Yeah, most of the shootings—
—Because it’s also a massive mistake or, I don’t know if you want to call it a mistake, but it should not happen, ever.
It should never happen. Pretty much.
Yeah, exactly.

Have to be pretty extraordinary circumstances. But it’s relatively rare. So the absolute numbers are fairly low. It’s about—depending on the year—it could be anywhere from 500 to 1,000 people a year are killed by police. Most of those—like 700, 800—are armed suspects, and then there’s a couple hundred that are unarmed.
It’s amazing, though, that we consider that a low number. It’s just like, by comparison—

—I know. It’s just crazy high when you compare it to other countries, which is another angle here. It’s orders of magnitude higher than, say, the UK, for example. In that group, the researchers basically said, "We can’t draw any conclusions. There’s just way too little data to do statistical analysis." The researchers themselves were very clear to say, even in the shooting data, that even where it showed—Again, it failed to show that there was a racial difference as an independent variable. But you always have to be careful when a study fails to show a relationship because it could always be that it just wasn’t a powerful enough study, like there wasn’t enough data to show, to statistical significance, that the effect was there. And that’s basically what the researcher was saying: "It’s not that we proved there isn’t; it’s just that, in this data, we couldn’t say that there was." But it’s hard to know how generalizable is this data, and if it’s just that a more robust data set would be able to show it. And they couldn’t even make any statements about the shooting of unarmed suspect because that was way too little data, statistically.
And we have to remember, too, a couple of things: (1) this is aggregate data, so we know that there are pockets, like Minneapolis—
—Absolutely.
—or Minnesota as a whole, right, where we’re seeing significant difference in the number—
—So, yeah. Exactly. There are some regional differences. For Minnesota, for example—or I think it says "Minneapolis"—in Minneapolis—
—Yeah, I think it’s just Minneapolis.

—the police use of nonlethal force is seven times higher, controlling for these other variables—meaning, like number of interactions with the police—seven times higher for African Americans than it is for Caucasians. And so that’s dramatic. That’s obviously going to vary region by region. And, of course, a lot of people cite the figure that if you’re a Black, you’re 2.5 times more likely to be killed by police than if you’re White, just to get the risk of, like—
—Right, because they’re also looking at the population. There’s only—
—That’s federal-level data.
Yeah, because 13% of the general population is Black, and so if the number is the same, then that means more Black people are getting killed.
Yeah, it’s per capita.
Per capita!
The lifetime risk for a Black male getting killed by the police is one in a thousand, which is not insignificant, and it’s also one of the higher causes of death for young African American males.

Ugh. And also just going to jail, like you see that those [numbers] are really, really high. But the other thing, I think, that’s not left out but that’s important to remember—and again, I’m not saying this—you could very easily, I think I’m being conspiratorial, but I’m not—there is no incentive to be candid about force, right?
Mmhmm.
Police are only going to report the minimum of what they have to report by law if they’re even being scrupulous.
I totally agree. I mean, of course! Of course they are.

Just like every single time a police officer kills somebody who’s unarmed, the original report almost always says it’s in self-defense first or that "they saw a weapon" or that whatever—there’s always reasoning that’s built into the report that then later is disproved.
Yeah. Now that we’re getting a lot of video evidence—
—Mmhmm.
—the data is shifting, definitely
So we have to remember that, too, the data is probably charitable at best.
But even if we take it at face value—so let’s just do this.
Sure.

Let’s be charitable and say, "All right. This data is accurate for what it is." And even given all the caveats let’s just assume I take it at face value. What would that mean about policing in the United States? First of all it does not mean, in my opinion, it does not mean that there isn’t an issue of [systemic] racism in policing because, again, the evidence from the nonlethal use of force is the most clear, and clearly shows that there’s a racial bias as an independent variable. And it also doesn’t capture a lot of things that wouldn’t necessarily be considered "use of force", just like pulling somebody over who’s "driving while black", things like that. You turn—
—And there are so many studies of those things—
—Yes. Absolutely.
—that show, over and over, that Blacks are significantly more likely to get pulled over—
—Stop and frisk.
—stop and frisk, have their cars searched, have to just get handcuffed and then released; there are a lot of studies on traffic stops and things like that.
A lot of the emails that we’ve been getting indicate that, I think, that there’s a misunderstanding by what we mean by [systemic] racism. That doesn’t mean that every cop is racist. It in fact—
—It doesn’t even mean that any cop is racist.
—It specifically means that that’s not the case. It just means that there are factors at work that make the experience of Black Americans with police different, [systemically] different—
—Worse!

—in a bad way, yeah—than White Americans. And it could be partly just socioeconomic. Historical factors come in to play: under-policing and over-policing in different neighborhoods, the neighborhoods themselves, the effects of red-lining over decades, things like that. And so all of that comes into play. There’s all these societal disparities. But the problem is that policing seems to be magnifying those societal disparities, when, in fact, if anything, it should be doing the opposite. It should be seeking to mitigate or minimize them.

Right. I think I saw a really good tweet that somebody wrote—I can’t remember—a social media post that said, and I’m paraphrasing, but something along the lines of "Institutional racism doesn’t mean that everybody in the institution is racist. That means that even if there were no racist people in the institution, it would still negatively harm Black people."
It’s just the way things are done.
That’s the point.
Yeah, absolutely.
The system itself has—
—It’s baked in.
—racist shit built into it.

I think the other big issue, here, is just that the use of force by American police compared to our industrialized nations' colleagues is orders of magnitude greater, and we need to figure out why that is; how much of that is just, again, the culture of policing; how much of it is the gun culture that we have in our country, always raising the stakes; how much of it is how policing is organized and structured and what’s required of them. So—
—Yeah, the militarization of the police forces. I think there’s a lot of argumentation around that being a huge problem—
—Yes. Absolutely.
—is that if you’ve got a hammer, everything’s going to be a nail. Well, if you’ve got tanks and automatic weapons, you might need to find an excuse to use them.

Yeah, there’s two factors, I think, that are playing into that. One is that in areas where social problems go out of control—like we have an opiate problem, a drug abuse problem, we’re not really taking care of the mentally ill, we’ve deinstitutionalized a lot of mentally ill [people]—that increases the societal demands on a city, a county, a state, and a lot of that falls to the police. And so they are, then, being stretched thin and being sort of the first line dealing with things like mental illness, and that creates this revolving door approach. And this something that we’ve talked about or has been talked about for decades, literally, since—
—Everything that falls through the cracks falls on their shoulders.

—And I’ve seen this personally as a physician. I’ve had patients who are caught in this cycle. You’re mentally ill. You create a disturbance or you threaten somebody or an incident. The police respond. What can they do? The only thing they really can do is arrest you, so they do. You go to prison, right? And then, when you’re done with prison, you go to a hospital. And then they treat you temporarily, but then they have no place to send you, so then you go back out on the street until you commit another offense. And you get arrested again. And that cycle—

—Yeah. Once you’ve been arrested, you’re completely disincentivized from entering society. You would think that everything is rehabilitative, but it’s actually a massive block to reentering society. You can’t get funding. You can’t get housing. You can’t get educational loans. You can’t get a good job, especially if you’re a felon. And, unfortunately, our drug laws—which have been historically also very racist—they breed felons, non-violent felons.

Yep. So you end up with the problem of mental illness being dealt with in the criminal legal system, with police sort of on the front lines, and then you have, combined with that, again, this militarization of police, which has been shown to increase the use of force by police. There are studies which showed that. And so, anyway, we have to—there’s a lot of recommendations about what we can do to improve the situation. So I just made a list of the most common ones that I’ve been seeing out there: ban choke holds; ban "no-knock warrants"; rebalance qualified immunity, which means—right now, police are almost immune from being sued for abuse of their power, their authority; a national registry of police offenders so they can’t just go to the next department; emphasize deescalation in police training, police use of force as a last result; police must report every time they draw their weapon or point a weapon at a civilian; mandated use of body cameras; better data collection across the board for all forms of police use of force. So you’ll notice that none of those have anything to do directly with race. This is all just about deescalating and reducing police use of force.

And, of course, if we could get it down to levels that are comparable to other, similar countries, or just to much lower levels, that will reduce, in absolute numbers, any use of force against historically oppressed populations and magnifying any implicit rational biases that are in the system, et cetera, et cetera. So it’s all good. But, in addition, there are some specifically race-focused recommendations like, "Yeah, you probably should make an effort so that the police force reflects the demographics of the community it’s policing." It’s probably a good thing.
Yeah. But there’s also good research to show that that’s not—it’s not enough. It doesn’t—

—It’s not enough. Absolutely. There’s no single panacea.[v 3] But we definitely have to get away from—listen, we’re not trying to say that individual police officers are bad people or [that] they’re any different than the population in general. It’s just people in that situation. And maybe we do need to think how they’re being structured, how they’re being trained, what kind of resources that they have. And I think we really, really, really need to emphasize how to minimize excessive use of force by our police. Systemically.

Like incentivization structures, code of silence issues, things like that, which have, historically, been really, really problematic. This idea that when something bad happens—I mean, you saw it in the video of the old man who was knocked down, and another cop was like, "Should we"—he reached for him, and the other cop pulled him away. And you also saw it in George Floyd’s video, when the cop had his knee on his neck and the other cop was like "Should we, like, roll him over?" And he was like, "No." It’s this culture of silence, complicity. These kinds of things have to change and, unfortunately, sometimes, this is why I think you’re seeing a lot of the protesters talking about "defunding" the police; it doesn’t mean "disband" the police. It means take some of the money that we’re putting towards police efforts and put them into social systems, or social programs.
Just completely restructure it. So I was very interested—
—Or restructure, yeah.

—in the Camden, New Jersey, experience, which was done under a Republican governor. They basically dissolved the police and then reconstituted them in order to restructure them from the ground up. And they focused on community-based policing. And the crime rate plummeted. So that’s the thing. It’s not just that we’re reducing police use of force. It’s actually better for the community. There’s lower crime. So this idea of like, "What do you want?"
Absolutely.
"You need to have aggressive, militarized police in order to reduce crime." No! It’s the opposite. It actually worsens the situation.
Yeah. That exacerbates it. It instigates it. It makes people more twitchy. It makes people more afraid to actually call the police.
Right.
Obviously there’s a long history of distrust, for good reason.
Right.
They’re looked at as almost like a paramilitary organization.
Oh, absolutely.
That’s not a good way of looking at that. I mean, it’s bad.
I would like to get beyond this, sort of, confrontational, either-or thing: you either support the police or you don’t, or whatever.
I know.
Yeah.

No, it’s that we want everyone to be functioning better. We want it to make lives better for the police and for all the citizens and, of course, we want to minimize and eradicate any inequities in the system. Racism, sexism, whatever. And we can do all of that. We can accomplish all of that. This is a situation—again, to be positive—it seems like we’re at a moment, at least, where there’s bipartisan support—
—Mmhmm.
—for a lot of specific fixes—
—Changes. Yeah. And accountability!

—We actually know what to do. We actually know what to do now. It’s not like we’re not sure what to do about it. Anyway, so I’m hoping that we’ll see some—and there are things winding their way through Congress. And we’ll see what happens.
That would be great.

But I just want to emphasize one big misconception, just to drive this point home. Saying that there is systemic racism in policing doesn’t mean we have to read the mind of one cop and say that they had racial animus or intent in a specific act that they did. That’s not what we mean. That’s not what we’re talking about.
No.

We’re just talking about all of these complex factors [conspiring] together to make the experience much worse for that segment of our population. And it’s really—it grinds people down in such a way that it’s horrible. And it needs to stop, and we could make it stop. And that needs to be a priority.

You know there’s a—coming in, as I always do, with the doc recommendations—there’s a great doc on PBS right now. The doc is called "The Talk." And what it’s really about is the talk, sadly, that African-American mothers have to have with their boys about how to conduct themselves—
—Yeah, I’ve read about that.
—When they are pulled over—
—Oh, wow.
—inevitably. Like what do you do to not get killed. And the thing is, we are privileged that we don’t have to have those kinds of conversations.
I’ve seen a lot of interviews with athletes, among other people, who have all alluded to that very thing.

Mmhmm. And it’s just really emotional, but it’s also really telling about these everyday individual experiences that you’re talking about, Steve, that add up to this concept that we are talking about of systemic racism in policing. So I highly recommend it because it just gives you, I think, a little bit more of that emotional connection to the problem, especially if you’re somebody who’s lucky enough to have never had to deal with it or think about it.
Yup.
Right.
Yup. Count our blessings, and try to be more empathetic, definitely.
All right, guys. Let’s go on with Science or Fiction.
Voice-over: It's time for Science or Fiction.
sections.title: Science or Fiction

sections.text: Each week I come up with three science news items or facts—two real and one fake—then I challenge my panel of skeptics to tell me which one is the fake! We have a theme this week. You guys might be familiar with the subject of the theme this week. The planet Earth. You guys have been to the planet Earth, haven’t you?
Yes.
I live there!
Up until December 21st of ’12…
Right… (laughs)
All right.
I lived there until the end of 2019. I don’t know what goddamn we’re on now.
(Rogues Laugh)
"Mirror, Mirror Earth" of some sort.
All right. Just three pretty much random facts about the Earth. You ready?
Yeah.
(silly voice) "Random."
Yeah.

Here we go! Item #1: About 50% of the heat given off by the Earth’s interior is generated from radioactive decay. Item #2: Earth is the densest planet in the Solar System. And Item #3: The driest place on Earth is the Atacama Desert in Chile and Peru, which receives, on average, 15 mm of rainfall per year. Who hasn’t gone first in a while? Cara?
(whispers) Dammit. I was so quiet, too.
(Rogues Laugh)
Cara, go first.

Okay. 50% of the heat is radioactive decay. I mean, I don’t know, is that a thing? Like, isn’t that what happens when the heavy elements break down into lighter elements, and they give off stuff? Is that part of radioactive decay? I feel like that’s a part of it. Earth is the densest—this one seems not real to me. "Earth is the densest planet in the Solar System?" See, now I have to compare all the other planets. The gas giants are big but they’re light. And, then, the rocky things are heavy, and we’re the biggest rocky thing, right? Right?
(laughs)

And so there’s probably other denser moons and stuff, but that’s tricky because you’re only talking about planets, and as of now, there’s only eight planets. And then "the driest place on Earth is the Atacama Desert:" I think I’m almost positive that that is science, but I have no idea if 15 millimeters is the right amount of rainfall. I’m going to assume that that’s not a multi-parter, where it was true except for this one small thing, and say that that’s science. So, is the Earth the densest planet, or is 50% of the heat given off generated from radioactive decay? No, I’ll say that the radioactive decay one’s the fiction. That Earth is the densest planet and the radioactive decay one—there’s another reason that heat is given off.
Okay. Jay?

I do know that the Earth is generating heat because of friction that happens way down near the Earth’s core and everything. But I do think that a good amount of heat comes from the radioactive decay. It’s just whether or not it’s 50%. So I will come back to that one. "Earth is the densest planet in the Solar System." Yeah, that one, I think, is true, and it’s one of those things that’s kind of just floating in the back of my head, you know, Cara, like, you’re like, "I think that’s true," and you don’t know why.
Yeah. I don’t know. Seems right… (laughs)

"The driest place on Earth"—you literally could have made up a word, and I would have believed you. There’s lots of super dry places on Earth. I thought that the North and South Poles were also considered to be extraordinarily dry. I’m going to say that the last one, the one about the driest place, is fiction just because I think I have a good chance of just, statistically, that he just made up a place.
All right. Bob, go next.
You know, every damn one of these seems wrong.
(Rogues Laugh)

50% of the heat…Earth’s interior—yeah, radioactive decay definitely keeps it molten, but my sense is that it’s already molten, and there’s a lot of heat, and the stuff that’s actually causing heat by the radioactive decay is less. It’s a small part of that. And then there’s this second one, "the densest planet in the Solar System." Sure, I mean the gas giants are, generally, not dense, overall. Saturn could literally float—if an ocean were big enough, it would literally float. It’s less dense than water. But, then again, most of the Earth is molten. Does that mean that it’s less dense than, say, Mars, that does not have such a huge molten core or mantle? That might make me pick Mars. But what about Venus? I don’t know about the core of Venus.
Dammit, Bob! How do you not know this? You’re supposed to know this!
Shit! I know!
Yeah, Bob!
(laughs)

See. Here’s a situation where I know too damn much about these stupid little things. And "the driest place on Earth…Atacama Desert"—Jay’s right. I mean, the driest place I’ve heard is the South Pole, Antarctica, because it doesn’t get hardly any precipitation throughout the course of the year. So I’ve heard that that was the driest place. I can make an argument for all of these.
(laughs)
All right. I’m going to go with #3, the Atacama Desert, only because I think I specifically remember reading, years ago, that the South Pole is driest place.
Okay.
Ugh!
And Evan?
Not to—I’ll try to—
—You sound too happy there, Steve! You sounded too happy.
—I’ll try go—Steve, can you define the Earth’s interior for the purposes of this?
So, in other words, not like radiating heat in the atmosphere from the Sun; it’s heat from within the Earth, itself.
Okay. So—
—There’s a different heat cycle, in terms of heat onto the Earth and being radiated away. This is heat from within the Earth leaving the Earth.
So I don’t have to think about the layers of the Earth: the upper crust, the lower crust, the mantle, and all that stuff? I can—
(shrugging shoulders with his voice) I don’t know.
—All that is considered Earth’s interior, for this purpose?
Yeah.
Below the ground.

Okay. I have a feeling this one’s going to turn out to be right. Now Earth being the densest planet—wouldn’t Mercury be the densest planet 'cause it’s so close to the Sun? I mean, the forces that would crush that rocky little thing into a tight wad, essentially?
Ohhhh.

(straining) So, Mercury, I don’t know. Gosh, it’s either that one or the driest place on Earth. Bob and Jay, I think, are pulling me into this one. I think without Bob and Jay’s help, I must admit, I may have gone with Earth being densest planet as the fiction, but I’ll say "Chile, Peru"—I’ll say that one’s the fiction.
(happily) All right. So you all agree that the Earth—
—He sounds really happy right now. (Laughs) Yup.
Oh, gosh!
Damn happy.
—that the Earth is the densest planet in the Solar System.
Is it Mercury?
You all agree that that one is science. And that one…is…science!
It is!?
Okay.
Oh, wow.

That is science. It is. The Earth is the densest planet. Yeah. You guys are basically right. Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars are all roughly the same amount of density, and then the gas giants are all much less dense 'cause they’re mostly gas, with Saturn being the lightest one and actually being less dense than water—1 gram per cubic centimeter.
I heard that somewhere.
So, yeah, Mercury: 5.427 [g/cm3]. Earth: 5.515. Venus: 5.243. And Mars is 3.933. Mars is the lightest of the four inner rocky worlds.
Really?
Yeah. So Mars is the lightest; Earth is the heaviest of those four.
Interesting.
Saturn’s the lightest overall.
It’s interesting. Yeah. There must be more material, just, physically, more material on the Earth than the other [three] interior planets—that that contributes to that?
Well, I mean, it is—
—We have a lot of water too.
—It is the biggest, and so the gravity would condense it more. That may be that.
Yeah. To crush—the pressure is at the core. That’s true.

All right. So let’s go back to #1: about 50% of the heat given off by the Earth’s interior is generated from radioactive decay. Cara, you think this one is the fiction. The guys think this one is science. And this one…is…science.
Yeah!
Woo-hoo!
Aw, shit.
It sounded science-y.
So it is the poles?
It is the poles. Yeah, but we’ll get there.
Yeah.
So this was based upon a study from a couple years ago, where they looked at—Bob, what do you think they were looking at?
Looking at the core? The core of the Earth?
Antineutrinos.
Oh-ho! Antineutrinos.
Antineutrinos?
Who’s anti-neutrinos?

They’re also calling [them] geoneutrinos. Ever hear that term before, geo—These are antielectron neutrinos. They are generated by radioactive decay in the Earth’s crust: mostly uranium, some thorium, and some potassium—
—I love thorium.

—Potassium-40. From that they were able to estimate how much of that radioactive decay is happening, and then, from that, how much heat would that release. And that accounts for about half of the heat that is radiating from the Earth itself. Again, not the heat that’s coming from the Sun but just from coming from inside the Earth. So that is, how much would say, if you had put a—it’s like one of those massive figures you could never guess on your own?
Wait. What is what? What are you asking?
How much energy are we talking about? How much heat energy?
Oh. Pfft. I don’t even know.
25 peta-joules.
Yeah, like what do you even measure that in? Joules?
Yeah, what’s the unit?
Forty-four terawatts. Forty-four terawatts, which are joules per second. A watt is a joule per second.
Okay.
Yeah, 44 TW is the total, and about half of that, or 22 TW, is coming from the radioactive decay. Now, if you recall, if you recall Lord Kelvin, right—
—Yes! Yes. I do remember Lord Kelvin.
—Yeah, Lord Kelvin calculated—
—He kind of called it. He kind of called it.

No, no. He got it wrong. He calculated the age of the Earth based upon its current likely temperature and the temperature that it was when it formed. And, according to him, the Earth should only be tens of thousands of years old because—
—Ah. There you go.
Right. But, Steve, if you remember the history, the young whippersnapper—who was talking about how radioactive decay is responsible—he was extremely diplomatic when dealing with Lord Kelvin.
Yeah.
And he said, "Lord Kelvin, actually, kind of figured it out because Kelvin said, 'Unless there’s a process, a nuclear process we are unaware of—
—Right.
—the Earth’s core should be solid." So he kind of, very diplomatically, handed him a peace offering while wiping away his belief system—
—He gave him out?
—he thought was going on. Yeah, he gave him an out. And it was, actually, a really cool thing to do. So that’s what I meant.
Yeah. But the bottom line was if you didn’t know about radioactive decay—because he didn’t because it was before radioactive decay was discovered—
E&B: —Right.
—then you just calculate the temperature as thermodynamics, it seems like Earth should have already solidified by now.
Right. And the same with the Sun. As you calculate it as a burning ball of gas, there’s no way it’s going to last for hundreds of millions of years.
But now we know about nuclear fusion and radioactive decay.
Yes.

All right. All of this means that "the driest place on Earth is the Atacama Desert in Chile and Peru, which receives, on average, 15 mm of rainfall per year"—that is the fiction. The Atacama Desert is the second driest place—
(laughs)
Yeah.
—on Earth. It is the—
—Dammit! It’s the driest non-polar region.
Yes. It is the driest—
Yes!
—non-polar region. A lot of sources forget to put "non-polar" in there, which is why I thought it would be a good fiction.
It’s known as the driest place on Earth. That’s its moniker.
Yeah. Right.
(laughs) Dammit!
But only "non-polar." What is the driest place on Earth? You have get more specific than "Antarctica." It is Antarctica, but where in Antarctica?
Directly at the South Pole?
No. It’s the—
—the Ross Ice Shelf?
—the Dry Valleys. The Dry Valleys.
(chuckles) Hence the name.
There hasn’t been any rain there in two million years.
(laughs)
Hoo-hoo!
Well, what are they waiting for?
Two million years?!
Maybe tomorrow.
There’s no—
—How do they know that there was rain two million years ago?
—There’s no ice. Because there’s no ice there. There’s no ice. There’s no snow. If it had snowed in the last two million years, it would still be there. That’s why.
Right.
Well, how do they know it wasn’t more than two million years?
Well, I don’t know. I didn’t do that deep a dive.
It hasn’t rained in (small voice) at least two million years!

Maybe "at least" is two million—but that’s what they’re saying. We know, for the last two millions years, that there has been no precipitation there, to use Bob’s term. And it’s because of the atmospherics there. It’s so cold—"How cold is it?"—
(laughs)

—that any moisture in the air becomes really, really heavy and sinks down. So it never gets to that place, that valley. It can’t get over the mountain into that valley. So there’s never any water there. No precipitation.
Wait. So there’s no ice at all?
Yeah. It’s bare ground in the middle of the Antarctic [continent].
Weird! But it’s like perma—
—Wow. That’s awesome.
—Is it like permafrost ground?
No. It’s rock. You look at this satellite picture—
—Yeah. It’s have to be like rock because it’s still—
—It’s rock. Yeah, there’s no—
—because it’s still frozen rock, but with no ice in it.
There’s no snow, no ice. Yup.
Weird.
Yeah. Very cool. That’s the driest place. Zero—zero precipitation.
But that 15 mm—is that right for the Atacama?
That’s accurate. Yup. That’s accurate.
Okay.
Although some years it has very—it can go a couple years without rain, but that’s why I said "on average."
Yeah.
All right. Well, good job, guys.
Well, I was almost right. (Laughs)
Yeah. That was tricky. I admit. It was a little tricky, but it’s the Earth.
So, I was like, "Definitely the driest place on Earth." That’s the only one I know! (Laughs)
I know I first heard about the Atacama Desert because of a bit of pseudoscience that derives from there. You guys familiar with this?
No!
What?
This is the Two-Inch Alien. You guys ever seen—
—Oh, I remember that.
Oh, the little guy!
(crosstalk)
—this mummified alien from the Atacama Desert. But it’s probably just an abortion—
Aww.
Yeah, it’s a—
—that somebody discarded.
It’s a fetus. Yeah, for sure.
It’s a fetus.
Yeah.
It’s a fetus. Or it was a spontaneous abortion. But either way, it’s fetus. It’s a human fetus. There’s no question. But it—
—It’s not a fully—yeah, it’s not a tiny adult.
It’s not the star child, or some craziness?
No.
No. People wish it were an alien.
Not an alien. Not an alien.

Science is elegant and beautiful, but it requires an effort to understand. This is a golden opportunity to educate people. Any person with a scientific temperament, not necessarily a scientist, cannot support these types of messages.– Hasan Al Hariri, CEO of the Dubai Astronomy Group, when asked about the June 21, 2020, doomsday insanity[1]
Evan, give us a quote!

"Science is elegant and beautiful, but it requires an effort to understand. This is a golden opportunity to educate people. Any person with a scientific temperament, not necessarily a scientist, cannot support these types of messages." And that was said by Hasan Al Hariri, who’s the CEO of the Dubai Astronomy Group, when asked about the June 21, 2020, doomsday insanity.
Good on him.
And that’s awesome. It was very well said, and I’m very happy to know that there’s a Dubai Astronomy Group! Very, very cool.
Yeah.
Yeah. Their mission is to promote the study of astronomy and related fields in the Middle East and in that region of the world. So that’s really cool.
Awesome.
Love it.
Yeah. I like that quote.
Well, thank you all for joining me this week.
Any week, Steve!
Sure, man!
Any time you need me, man.
Thanks, Doc!
And we will see you on the Friday Live Stream—
Yeah! That’s great.
Yeah! Woo-hoo.
Oh yeah!
—The SGU has been live-streaming at 5 p.m. ET every week.
We’ll see you yesterday!
Yeah, we’re going to keep doing that for as long as we want to. So we’ll see you all there. And, until next week, this is your  Skeptics' Guide to the Universe.
